blocks.text: Many kinds of bacteria have flagella, which enable them to move. A secondary function of flagella is to detect and respond to chemical signals.

Bacteria are named by how their flagella are arranged. Bacteria that do not possess flagella are atrichous. Those with a single polar flagellum are monotrichous. Those with a tuft of flagella at one pole are lophotrichous. Those with flagella at each of the two poles are amphitrichous. Those with flagella surrounding the whole cell are peritrichous.

blocks.alt: Five rod-shaped cells in a row: atrichous with no flagella; monotrichous with one flagellum at one pole; lophotrichous with a tuft at one pole; amphitrichous with a flagellum at each pole; peritrichous with flagella all round the cell.
blocks.caption: The different arrangements of bacterial flagella (original diagram after Figure 2.7).
blocks.long_description: Each cell is a horizontal rod. The first has a plain surface. The second has one wavy flagellum from its right end. The third has four flagella fanning out from the right end. The fourth has one flagellum at each end. The fifth has flagella spread all around its surface.

blocks.text: The flagellum of bacteria is entirely different in structure from the flagellum of eukaryotes. It is not built on the 9 + 2 pattern of microtubules; it is composed of the protein flagellin. A bacterial flagellum consists of three parts: a basal body, a hook and a filament.

items: Basal body: present just beneath the cell membrane. It consists of rotating rings, one pair in Gram-positive bacteria and two pairs in Gram-negative bacteria. The rings anchor the flagellum in the cell membrane and the cell wall.
Hook: a curved structure that connects the basal body with the filament.
Filament: the long helical part made of flagellin that extends outside the cell.

blocks.alt: A bacterial flagellum in cross-section through the Gram-negative envelope: a long filament outside the cell joins a curved hook, which joins a basal body of a rod with two pairs of rings set in the outer membrane, the peptidoglycan layer and the cell membrane.
blocks.caption: Structure of the bacterial flagellum (original diagram after Figure 2.8).
blocks.long_description: From top to bottom: the filament, a long wavy line outside the cell; the hook, a short curved joint; the basal body, a vertical rod carrying ring pairs. The outer pair of rings sits in the outer membrane and the peptidoglycan layer; the inner pair sits in the cell membrane. The rings are what anchor the flagellum and let it rotate. A note says Gram-positive bacteria have only one pair of rings.

blocks.title: Pili
blocks.text: Some bacteria have pili (singular: pilus). These are non-helical, filamentous appendages, smaller and thinner than flagella. Pili are used for the attachment of bacteria to various surfaces, and they are also involved in the mating process (conjugation) between cells.
